extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, agency counsel, administrative-law practitioners, and public commenters on Clean Air Act rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-analytic criteria for evaluating whether the Major Questions Doctrine bars EPA from regulating greenhouse gases under Section 202(a), and related standards for lawful vehicle-emissions standard-setting under the Clean Air Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The major questions doctrine applies only to 'extraordinary cases' and is reserved for instances where an agency's assertion of authority is both unheralded and a 'transformative expansion' of its scope and where the asserted authority has profound economic and political significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Brown & Williamson, UARG, West Virginia, Nebraska. The doctrine is limited; a broader conception risks making the doctrine the rule rather than the exception. The Supreme Court has not applied the doctrine based on economic/political significance alone; it looks to history/breadth of asserted authority plus economic/political significance together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unheralded assertion of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: To trigger the major questions doctrine, the agency must be asserting a newfound, 'unheralded' authority—i.e., authority that was not previously claimed or consistently exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the agency and other branches have long recognized the authority (e.g., EPA has regulated GHGs under §202(a) for 15+ years; successive administrations have issued standards). Compare timing to cases where MQ applied (authority newly asserted 1–7 years before decisions). Consider congressional acquiescence and judicial recognition; if Congress and courts have repeatedly recognized the authority, it is not 'unheralded.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformative expansion of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency's action must effect a 'transformative expansion'—a change in kind (not merely degree) in the scope or nature of the delegated authority—to implicate the major questions doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the regulation changes the number/types of regulated sources or the traditional nature of agency decisionmaking. For §202(a), including greenhouse gases does not add new source categories (vehicles already emit multiple regulated pollutants) and so is a difference in degree, not kind. Distinguish technology-based, source-focused standards from regime-shifting actions like the generation-shifting regime at issue in West Virginia, which attempted to reorder the nationwide electric grid and compel sectoral shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and political significance must be different in kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Even significant economic or political consequences are insufficient by themselves to trigger the major questions doctrine; the consequences must be 'different in kind' from those posed by ordinary regulatory exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency seeking to rely on MQ must show vast economic and political consequences that are categorically distinct from other emissions regulations. Because many federal rules are economically and politically significant, relying on significance alone would improperly expand MQ. Courts have declined to apply MQ where historical precedent for the authority exists despite consequential effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider available and feasible technologies and related factors in standard-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: When setting standards under §202(a), EPA must consider available and feasible technologies and make findings on technology effectiveness and feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant factors include technology effectiveness; cost (including per vehicle, per manufacturer, and per purchaser); lead time necessary to implement the technology; the feasibility of potential standards; impacts on emissions reductions; impacts on oil conservation and energy security; impacts on fuel savings; impacts on vehicle manufacturing industry; and other factors such as impacts on safety. EPA has a longstanding practice of analyzing these factors and applying the same process for GHGs as for other pollutants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance-based standard does not equal a mandate to change product mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards that are performance-based do not require manufacturers to sell any particular mix of vehicles or to invest in other transportation modes; they set fleet-average emissions outcomes, leaving manufacturers to choose compliance pathways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the rule forces producers to stop producing certain products or to subsidize competitors; performance-based standards allow manufacturers to meet fleet averages through many technological or strategy choices. Historical examples: catalytic converters adoption, attribute-based standards preserving car/truck distinctions; EPA's prior findings that manufacturers would still produce gasoline vehicles under the challenged standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of electrification technologies is within statutory scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating increased electrification as an 'available technology' for preventing or controlling vehicular pollution is within §7521(a)'s statutory scope and does not transform EPA's authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice (e.g., National Low-Emission Vehicle Program 1997; multipollutant standards 2000 with zero-emission vehicle bin and credits) and EPA findings (standards achievable by ICE, HEV, PHEV, BEV technologies) support this. Electrification technologies are analogous to other electrical/aftertreatment technologies (catalytic converters, SCR, DPF). Courts have upheld standards premised on single known technologies; considering electrification is not per se novel or arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect impacts (fuel demand/infrastructure) are inherent and not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect impacts of vehicle emissions standards—such as effects on gasoline demand or fueling infrastructure—are inherent consequences of regulation and do not, by themselves, render a rule a transformative assertion of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: elimination of lead from gasoline, provisioning of DEF, introduction of low-sulfur diesel—regulation has long altered supporting infrastructure. To trigger MQ on this basis, the agency would have to show every conceivable §202(a) exercise regarding GHGs would produce extreme consequences different in kind from other pollutant regulations; ordinary indirect effects are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirement to consider source contribution and danger to health/welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202(a) requires EPA to consider a source's contribution to air pollution and determine whether that pollution poses a danger to human health and welfare when assessing the need for standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the same analysis applied to all pollutants; EPA may consider the 'totality of adverse impacts from climate change' insofar as the statute requires evaluating whether the source's contribution to aggregate pollution creates danger. Precedent and prior rulemaking (e.g., motorcycle, VOC/NOx/PM rules) show EPA can justify standards even where a source contributes a small fraction of total pollution.
